cells.tense: The connection is chosen and already running between the two of you.
cells.act: keep the heading when it is contested
cells.ask: When something pushes against the direction you two picked, say the heading once, plainly, and keep walking it.
cells.core:
The connection is chosen, and it is running. You and the other person are moving as one stream now, and the strength in you that holds its shape under weight is doing what it is for — letting the joining stand without stiffening into something brittle. There is real direction here, and you can feel your own part in it.

When something pushes against the direction the two of you picked, say the heading once, plainly, and stay on it. That is the whole practice. The push may come from a person outside it, or from the quiet of a tired week; either way your part is the same. You will learn by doing it how much of the heading is yours to carry and how much simply holds once it has been said.
cells.sheetLine: The direction holds when you name it once.
cells.verb: two streams meeting and choosing to flow as one
cells.place: in the strength that holds its shape under weight

cells.tense: You are guarding a joining that has not happened yet.
cells.act: rest in the result of the tending
cells.ask: Once this week, when you catch yourself bracing for a wrong turn that has not come, let the bracing go and rest ten minutes in what is already built between you.
cells.core:
The connection is chosen, but you are somewhere ahead of it, guarding a joining that has not happened yet. You read the future of it more than the present, and the strength that holds its shape under weight is gripping instead of bearing. From where you stand it feels like care. From outside, it can feel like a hand held too tight around something that was already standing.

For a week, the practice is smaller than it will feel: when you notice the bracing for a wrong turn that has not come, set it down and rest ten minutes in whatever already stands between you, however unfinished. No fixing, no review. What has grown between you keeps growing whether or not you watch it. You will find the joining sturdier than your watching ever made it.
cells.sheetLine: The joining is sturdier than your watching.
cells.verb: two streams meeting and choosing to flow as one
cells.place: in the strength that holds its shape under weight

cells.tense: You were part of a joining once, and you have not been in one since.
cells.act: list the pulls on you and mark which are yours
cells.ask: Take a page, name the things pulling at you right now, then put a mark beside each one saying whether it is yours.
cells.core:
There was a joining, and it is behind you now. Since then the strength that holds its shape under weight has been running on little, keeping things mostly by habit, and not much of what you carry is carrying you back. You can keep standing at a door that has already closed, and part of you does.

Here is something that asks almost nothing. Take a page and name everything pulling at you right now, however small. Then put a mark beside each one — mine, or came with someone else? The list does not need cleaning up, and nothing has to be done with it. It is only to let you see again the line between what is yours and what you have been holding on another person's behalf. That line is still there, and it is still yours to draw.

cells.tense: You are already held, and telling it as though you are not.
cells.act: point to the passage you can see
cells.ask: When someone says they are stuck somewhere you have already been, name the one step that worked for you and stop there.
cells.core:
The joining is here, and other people see it before you say it. When it comes up, you give it another name — luck, a season — and the strength that holds its shape under weight goes unnoticed even by you while it works. What holds the two of you together is partly yours, and your account leaves that out.

There is a small way back toward seeing it. When someone tells you they are stuck somewhere you have already been, name the one step that worked for you — once, in plain words — and then let the moment close. No follow-up, no checking. Saying the step aloud shows you that you know the route, and knowing you know it is what has been missing.
cells.sheetLine: You found a route. You just don't count it.

The asks survive being wrong: defending a heading, enjoying what grew, naming your own pull, and handing directions to one person are useful whether or not a merger is in progress. The sentence that serves me more than them is any line that describes the other person in the connection, so no cell describes anyone but the person drawing.
